The paper presents a new preconditioner for solving large-scale dense linear systems of equations arising from the discretization of boundary integral equations in electromagnetism.
The preconditioner is based on Frobenius-norm minimization and is inherently parallel.
The sparsity pattern of the preconditioner is computed adaptively during the computation of M itself or prescribed a priori based on some heuristics.
The criterion for selecting the nonzero structure of the column of the preconditioner is to retain all the edges within the box itself and one level of neighboring boxes.
The sparse approximate inverse preconditioner is less prone to instabilities than incomplete factorizations.
The tolerance for the iterative solution is 10^-3.
The level of accuracy of the matrix-vector product operation in the multipole code is estimated to be in the same order of magnitude as the relative error of the matrix-vector product operation.
The density of the sparse approximate inverse decreases for increasing problem size, leading to poor parallel scalability.
The implementation of the preconditioner shows very good parallel scalability, with an nlogn factor appearing in the results.

The paper presents results on the numerical scalability of the sparse approximate inverse preconditioner on a set of test problems arising from realistic radar cross-section (RCS) calculations in industry.
The results show that the preconditioner does not scale well with the problem size, especially for GMRES(120) on the Cetaf problem.
The solution time of full GMRES is strongly affected by the orthogonalisation involved in the Arnoldi procedure.
The use of larger restarts can reduce the solution time even though it significantly deteriorates the convergence.
The Airbus aircraft is very difficult to solve because the mesh has many surface details and the discretization matrices become ill-conditioned.
The linear systems arising from the CFIE formulation are much easier to solve than those from the EFIE formulation.
Preconditioned full GMRES converges in 24 iterations on the aircraft with more than a million degrees of freedom.
